question: A 16-year-old boy presents with sudden-onset severe left scrotal pain that woke him at night, with nausea and vomiting. The scrotum is swollen and tender. The cremasteric reflex is absent on the left. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Send a midstream urine and start empirical ciprofloxacin for epididymo-orchitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The absent cremasteric reflex in a teenager with sudden-onset severe scrotal pain strongly suggests torsion, not infection. Starting antibiotics and delaying surgery risks testicular necrosis.

answers.text: Arrange urgent scrotal Doppler ultrasound and wait for the result before deciding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Doppler ultrasound can support the diagnosis but must never delay surgery when torsion is clinically suspected. The salvage rate drops sharply after six hours; waiting for imaging is not safe.

answers.text: Take the patient to theatre immediately for scrotal exploration and bilateral orchidopexy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. An absent cremasteric reflex in an adolescent with sudden severe scrotal pain is torsion until proven otherwise. Urgent surgical exploration within six hours of onset is the only way to save the testis; bilateral orchidopexy is performed at the same time.

answers.text: Give analgesia and reassess in four hours to see whether the pain settles

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: A four-hour watch-and-wait approach is dangerous — after six hours of ischaemia the salvage rate falls below 50%; after 24 hours the testis is almost certainly non-viable.

overallFeedback.feedback: Testicular torsion is the priority diagnosis in any adolescent with sudden severe scrotal pain and an absent cremasteric reflex. Urgent exploration (not imaging, not antibiotics) is the only safe option — ischaemia is time-critical.
Correct. Absent cremasteric reflex + sudden severe scrotal pain in an adolescent = torsion until proven otherwise. Theatre immediately — salvage depends on speed.
